claim: Drosophila larvae produce two novel long-chain fatty acids that are attractive to other larvae: (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid
source: We found that larvae produce two novel long-chain fatty acids that are attractive to other larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical analysis data (GC-MS) showing these compounds in larval extracts and behavioral assays demonstrating attraction

claim: A single larval chemosensory neuron marked by R58F10 detects (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid
source: We identified a single larval chemosensory neuron that detects these molecules.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging showing R58F10 neurons respond to these pheromones and behavioral experiments showing silencing R58F10 blocks attraction

claim: Two members of the pickpocket family of DEG/ENaC channel subunits (ppk23 and ppk29) are required to respond to larval pheromones
source: Two members of the pickpocket family of DEG/ENaC channel subunits (ppk23 and ppk29) are required to respond to these pheromones.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing mutations in ppk23 and ppk29 block attraction to pheromones and calcium imaging showing mutant neurons do not respond

claim: The larval exudates of D. simulans are not attractive to other larvae
source: This pheromone system is evolving quickly, since the larval exudates of D. simulans, the sister species of D. melanogaster, are not attractive to other larvae.
evidence: Supported by behavioral assays showing D. simulans larvae are not attracted to conspecific residue

claim: Test larvae spent more time on larval-treated substrate than on untreated control substrate
source: We found that test larvae spent more time on the larval-treated substrate than on the untreated control substrate (Figure 1B), suggesting that the population of larvae had deposited an attractive pheromone on the substrate.
evidence: Supported by behavioral preference data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Silencing neurons expressing ppk23 with tetanus toxin blocked the response to larval cue
source: Silencing neurons expressing ppk23 with TNT blocked the response to the cue.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B showing reduced preference when ppk23-GAL4 drives TNT

claim: Mutations affecting ppk23 or ppk29 blocked attraction to larval cue
source: Mutations affecting ppk23 or ppk29 also blocked attraction.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B showing Δppk23 and Δppk29 mutants have reduced preference

claim: Silencing neurons with Janelia enhancer fragment R58F10-GAL4 blocked the response to larval cue
source: Silencing neurons with Janelia enhancer fragment R58F10-GAL4 blocked the response to the cue.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B showing reduced preference when R58F10-GAL4 drives TNT

claim: ppk23 expressing neurons innervate the terminal organ
source: ppk23 expressing neurons innervating the terminal organ (arrow), marked by membrane-targeted green fluorescent protein, mCD8:GFP (green, anti-GFP).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1D

claim: R58F10 sensory neurons innervate the terminal organ
source: R58F10 sensory neurons innervate the terminal organ (arrow).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1F

claim: R58F10 neuron synaptic terminals project into the suboesophageal zone
source: R58F10 neuron synaptic terminals project into the suboesophageal zone (arrow).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1G

claim: Blocking all olfactory neurons using Or83b-GAL4 did not block larval attraction to the cue
source: Blocking all olfactory neurons using Or83b-GAL4, or gustatory receptors implicated in pheromone responses with Gr32a-GAL4 and Gr33a-GAL4, or mutations affecting these genes, did not block larval attraction to the cue.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Hexane and acetone extracts of larval-treated glass elicited similar levels of attraction as plates treated directly with larvae
source: Hexane and acetone extracts elicited similar levels of attraction as plates treated directly with larvae.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2B

claim: Ethanol extracts did not elicit attraction
source: Ethanol extracts did not.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2B showing no preference for ethanol extracts

claim: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry of larval extracts revealed seven common saturated fatty acids and fatty acid derivatives and two rare fatty acid monoenes, (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid
source: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry of these extracts revealed that they contained seven common saturated fatty acids and fatty acid derivatives and two rare fatty acid monoenes, (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 2C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The adult sex pheromones (Z)-11-vaccenyl acetate (cVA), 7-tricosene, 7,11-heptocosadiene, or CH503 were not detected in larval extracts
source: We did not detect the adult sex pheromones (Z)-11-vaccenyl acetate (cVA), 7-tricosene, 7,11-heptocosadiene, or CH503 in these extracts.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS analysis of larval extracts

claim: (Z)-9-tetradecenoic acid was observed in extracts of whole larval bodies but not in significant levels in the residue deposited by larvae
source: While we observed (Z)-9-tetradecenoic acid in extracts of whole larval bodies, we did not observe significant levels of this compound in the residue deposited by larvae, suggesting that (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid are the major tetradecanoic derivatives deposited by larvae.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS analysis comparing whole body extracts to residue extracts

claim: (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid is found as a component of a defensive, ant-repulsive secretion released by some thrips
source: (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid is found also as a component of a defensive, ant-repulsive secretion released by some thrips (Suzuki et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suzuki et al., 2004

claim: (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid has not been found in any other insect
source: To our knowledge, (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid has not been found in any other insect.
evidence: Based on knowledge of existing literature

claim: Control larvae were attracted to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid, but not to any other compound at 50 fm/cm2
source: Control larvae were attracted to low concentrations (50 fm/cm2) of (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid, but not to any other compound (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Larvae showed a sustained response to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid over the entire duration of a 5-min assay
source: Moreover, larvae showed a sustained response to these two molecules over the entire duration of a 5-min assay (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Supported by time course data in Figure 2F,G

claim: (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid are strongly attractive to larvae across a broad range of concentrations
source: Dose response curves revealed that (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid are strongly attractive to larvae across a broad range of concentrations (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data in Figure 2H

claim: Larvae responded most strongly to pheromone concentrations of 50 fm/cm2 and this effect decreased at higher concentrations
source: Larvae responded most strongly to pheromone concentrations of 50 fm/cm2 and this effect decreased at higher concentrations.
evidence: Supported by dose-response data in Figure 2H

claim: Larvae were attracted to a blend of (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid, but were less responsive to this mixture than to a presentation of each molecule alone
source: Larvae were attracted to a blend of these compounds, but were less responsive to this mixture than to a presentation of each molecule alone, which suggests an interaction between the two pheromones (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2I,J

claim: Silencing R58F10 neurons with tetanus toxin blocked larval attraction to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid, (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid, and a mixture of the two pheromones
source: Silencing R58F10 neurons with tetanus toxin blocked larval attraction to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid, (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid, and a mixture of the two pheromones, but had no significant effect on the response to the other compounds at 50 fmol/cm2 (Figure 2E,I).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2E,I

claim: R58F10 neurons were excited in response to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid at 0.01 nM, 1 nM, and 100 nM
source: R58F10 neurons were excited in response to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid at 0.01 nM, 1 nM, and 100 nM.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3B

claim: R58F10 neurons were not significantly excited by (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid at 0.01 nM, but responded to higher concentrations
source: R58F10 neurons were not significantly excited by (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid at 0.01 nM, but responded to higher concentrations (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3A,B

claim: At 1 nM, R58F10 neurons exposed to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid or (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid were strongly elevated in their integrated fluorescence over the length of the trial compared to vehicle controls
source: Moreover, at 1 nM, which corresponds to the concentration that evoked the peak behavioral preference (Figure 2H), R58F10 neurons exposed to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid or (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid were strongly elevated in their integrated fluorescence over the length of the trial compared to vehicle controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3C

claim: R58F10 neurons were not excited by tetradecanoic acid, (Z)-9-octadecanoic acid, nor by vehicle controls
source: R58F10 neurons were not excited by tetradecanoic acid, which lacks a double bond compared to these pheromones, by (Z)-9-octadecanoic acid, a structurally similar, but longer, fatty acid monoene, nor by vehicle controls (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3A-C

claim: Both (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid elicited activity in at least one of the two neurons marked by Gr33a-GAL4 that innervate the dorsolateral terminal organ sensillum
source: Both (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid elicited activity in at least one of these neurons (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3D,E

claim: Silencing ppk23-GAL4 expressing neurons with tetanus toxin reduced larval attraction to both (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid compared to control larvae
source: As expected, silencing ppk23-GAL4 expressing neurons with tetanus toxin reduced larval attraction to both (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 4A,B) and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 4E,F) compared to control larvae.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4A,B,E,F

claim: Removing ppk23 gene function reduced the attraction of larvae to both (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid compared to heterozygous controls
source: Removing ppk23 gene function also reduced the attraction of larvae to both of these compounds compared to heterozygous controls (Figure 4A,C,E,G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4A,C,E,G

claim: The expression of ppk23 in R58F10 cells partially restored the attraction of larvae to both larval pheromones in a Δppk23 mutant background
source: The expression of ppk23 in R58F10 cells partially restored the attraction of larvae to both larval pheromones (Figure 4A,D,E,H).
evidence: Supported by behavioral rescue data in Figure 4A,D,E,H

claim: Larvae homozygous for a deletion of ppk29 were not attracted to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid
source: Larvae homozygous for a deletion of ppk29 were not attracted to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 4I,J)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4I,J

claim: Larvae homozygous for a deletion of ppk29 displayed weaker attraction to (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid than did heterozygous control larvae
source: Larvae homozygous for a deletion of ppk29 were not attracted to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 4I,J) and displayed weaker attraction to (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 4L,M) than did heterozygous control larvae.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4L,M

claim: The expression of ppk29 in R58F10 cells did not rescue the attraction of larvae to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid
source: The expression of ppk29 in R58F10 cells did not rescue the attraction of larvae to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 4I,K)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4I,K

claim: The expression of ppk29 in R58F10 cells partially restored the attraction of larvae to (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid
source: The expression of ppk29 in R58F10 cells did not rescue the attraction of larvae to (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 4I,K), but partially restored the attraction of larvae to (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 4L,N).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 4L,N

claim: R58F10 neurons mutant for either ppk23 or ppk29 were not excited by 1 nM (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid nor by (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid
source: R58F10 neurons mutant for either ppk23 or ppk29 were not excited by 1 nM (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid nor by (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid (Figure 4O,P).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 4O,P

claim: D. sechellia larvae are attracted to substrate treated with conspecific larvae
source: We found that third instar D. sechellia larvae are attracted, and D. simulans larvae are not attracted, to substrate treated with conspecific larvae (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5

claim: D. simulans larvae are not attracted to substrate treated with conspecific larvae
source: We found that third instar D. sechellia larvae are attracted, and D. simulans larvae are not attracted, to substrate treated with conspecific larvae (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5

claim: D. simulans larvae are attracted to residues produced by D. melanogaster and D. sechellia
source: D. simulans larvae were as attracted to these residues, as were D. melanogaster and D. sechellia (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A

claim: D. simulans larvae were attracted to synthetic (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid
source: Furthermore, D. simulans larvae were attracted to synthetic (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid, and their preference was indistinguishable from the attraction of D. melanogaster and D. sechellia to these molecules (Figure 2E, Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2E, Figure 5A, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Both D. melanogaster and D. sechellia larvae were indifferent to D. simulans residue, but were attracted to D. sechellia residue
source: We found that both D. melanogaster and D. sechellia larvae were indifferent to D. simulans residue, but were attracted to D. sechellia residue (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A

claim: Extracts from glass treated with D. simulans larvae were not attractive to wild-type D. melanogaster larvae
source: Extracts from glass treated with D. simulans larvae were not attractive to wild-type D. melanogaster larvae.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A

claim: Both D. sechellia hexane and acetone extracts were attractive to wild-type D. melanogaster larvae
source: In contrast, both D. sechellia hexane and acetone extracts were attractive to wild-type D. melanogaster larvae (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A

claim: Levels of both (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid are reduced in D. simulans relative to D. sechellia and D. melanogaster
source: We found that levels of both (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid and (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid are reduced in D. simulans relative to D. sechellia and D. melanogaster (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS quantification data in Figure 5B,C

claim: Acetone extract of D. simulans larval residue was mildly repulsive to D. simulans larvae
source: This hypothesis was supported, initially, by the observation that acetone extract of D. simulans larval residue was mildly repulsive to D. simulans larvae (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 6B,C

claim: While (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid alone was attractive to D. simulans, this activity was blocked completely by the addition of D. simulans extract
source: While (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid alone was attractive to D. simulans, this activity was blocked completely by the addition of D. simulans extract (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 6B,D

claim: The addition of (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid to D. simulans extract partially rescued the attraction of D. simulans to the extract, but not to the level observed for (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid tested alone
source: In contrast, the addition of (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid to D. simulans extract partially rescued the attraction of D. simulans to the extract, but not to the level observed for (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid tested alone (Figure 6B,E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 6B,E

claim: While D. simulans larvae were attracted to a mixture of the two pheromones alone, the addition of both pheromones to D. simulans extract conferred no attractive activity
source: Last, while D. simulans larvae were attracted to a mixture of the two pheromones alone, the addition of both pheromones to D. simulans extract conferred no attractive activity (Figure 6B,F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 6B,F

claim: Pheromones mediate many insect social behaviors, including navigation and aggregation
source: Pheromones, chemical signals that convey social information, mediate many insect social behaviors, including navigation and aggregation.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about pheromones

claim: Several studies have suggested that behavior during the immature larval stages of Drosophila development is influenced by pheromones, but none of these compounds or the pheromone-receptor neurons that sense them have been identified
source: Several studies have suggested that behavior during the immature larval stages of Drosophila development is influenced by pheromones, but none of these compounds or the pheromone-receptor neurons that sense them have been identified.
evidence: Based on inference from prior literature

claim: Pheromones mediate courtship, aggression, alarm signaling, parental care, navigation, aggregation and many other behaviors in insects
source: For example, pheromones mediate courtship, aggression, alarm signaling, parental care, navigation, aggregation and many other behaviors (Shorey, 1973; de Bruyne and Baker, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shorey, 1973 and de Bruyne and Baker, 2008

claim: The use of chemical cues is widespread amongst insects and other taxa, including mammals
source: While the use of chemical cues is widespread amongst insects (Symonds and Elgar, 2008) and other taxa, including mammals (Dulac and Torello, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Symonds and Elgar, 2008 and Dulac and Torello, 2003

claim: The majority of our understanding of the molecular and neural mechanisms that mediate insect pheromone signaling has come from studies of Drosophila melanogaster
source: the majority of our understanding of the molecular and neural mechanisms that mediate insect pheromone signaling has come from studies of a single species, Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Most studies of pheromones in Drosophila have focused on pheromones related to sex
source: Most studies of pheromones in Drosophila have focused on pheromones related to sex (Dahanukar and Ray, 2011; Fernández and Kravitz, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dahanukar and Ray, 2011 and Fernández and Kravitz, 2013

claim: Pheromones that organize spatial behaviors like navigation or aggregation have been less intensively studied in Drosophila
source: In contrast, pheromones that organize spatial behaviors like navigation or aggregation have been less intensively studied in Drosophila (Bartelt et al., 1985)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bartelt et al., 1985

claim: Ants employ substrate-born pheromones to establish and maintain foraging trails
source: For example, ants employ substrate-born pheromones to establish and maintain foraging trails (Steck, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Steck, 2012

claim: Caterpillars use pheromones to organize mass migrations
source: caterpillars use pheromones to organize mass migrations (Fitzgerald, 1976, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fitzgerald, 1976, 2003

claim: Drosophila larvae are robustly attracted to odors produced by other larvae in food
source: First, Drosophila larvae are robustly attracted to odors produced by other larvae in food (Durisko and Dukas, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Durisko and Dukas, 2013

claim: When in close proximity on a food source, larvae both aggregate and engage in a form of co-operative digging
source: Second, when in close proximity on a food source, larvae both aggregate (Durisko et al., 2014) and engage in a form of co-operative digging, which may effectively increase their rate of feeding (Wu et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Durisko et al., 2014, Wu et al., 2003, and Xu et al., 2008

claim: In natural conditions, larvae preferentially pupariate with conspecific larvae and avoid pupariating with larvae of other species
source: Finally, in natural conditions, where different species of drosophilids can be found sharing the same food resource, larvae preferentially pupariate with conspecific larvae and avoid pupariating with larvae of other species (Beltramí et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beltramí et al., 2012

claim: Many insects employ fatty acid derived pheromones in the context of aggregation and navigation
source: Many insects employ fatty acid derived pheromones in the context of aggregation and navigation
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: ppk23 and ppk29 play broad, non-redundant roles in sex pheromone-mediated behaviors, courtship and aggression
source: These genes play broad, non-redundant roles in sex pheromone-mediated behaviors, courtship and aggression, and are required for detecting the male pheromones, cVA, (Z)-5-pentacosene, and (Z)-7-tricosene, and the female pheromones, 7,11-heptacosadiene and 7,11-nonacosadiene (Lu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2012; Yuan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2012; Yuan et al., 2013

claim: ppk23 and ppk29 are required for detecting the male pheromones cVA, (Z)-5-pentacosene, and (Z)-7-tricosene, and the female pheromones 7,11-heptacosadiene and 7,11-nonacosadiene
source: These genes play broad, non-redundant roles in sex pheromone-mediated behaviors, courtship and aggression, and are required for detecting the male pheromones, cVA, (Z)-5-pentacosene, and (Z)-7-tricosene, and the female pheromones, 7,11-heptacosadiene and 7,11-nonacosadiene (Lu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2012; Yuan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012; Toda et al., 2012; Yuan et al., 2013

claim: Members of the pickpocket family form heteromeric protein complexes
source: Members of this family form heteromeric protein complexes (Eskandari et al., 1999; Benson and et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eskandari et al., 1999 and Benson et al., 2002

claim: ppk29 is expressed more broadly than initially characterized
source: Recent work has demonstrated that ppk29 is expressed more broadly than initially characterized, and that ppk29 mRNA regulates a second channel gene (seizure) to control membrane excitability of motor neurons through a protein independent mechanism (Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2014

claim: ppk29 mRNA regulates a second channel gene (seizure) to control membrane excitability of motor neurons through a protein independent mechanism
source: Recent work has demonstrated that ppk29 is expressed more broadly than initially characterized, and that ppk29 mRNA regulates a second channel gene (seizure) to control membrane excitability of motor neurons through a protein independent mechanism (Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2014

claim: The adult male-derived sex pheromone cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA) is detected by Or65a/Or67d-expressing olfactory receptor neurons
source: This is the adult male-derived sex pheromone cis-vaccenyl acetate (cVA) and the Or65a/Or67d-expressing olfactory receptor neurons that signal both female attractiveness and elicit male–male aggression in adult flies.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: cVA is a volatile pheromone, and its detection is processed via the DA1 glomerulus in the antennal lobe
source: cVA is a volatile pheromone, and its detection is processed via the DA1 glomerulus in the antennal lobe (Fernández and Kravitz, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fernández and Kravitz, 2013

claim: Contact-mediated pheromones are detected by gustatory neurons and the signals are processed in the subesophagael zone and ventral nerve cord
source: These pheromones, unlike cVA, are detected by gustatory neurons and the signals are processed in the subesophagael zone and ventral nerve cord (Thorne et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thorne et al., 2004

claim: D. simulans and D. sechellia diverged from D. melanogaster approximately 3–5 MYA
source: These species diverged from D. melanogaster approximately 3–5 MYA and diverged from each other approximately 0.5 MYA (Kliman et al., 2000; Lachaise and Silvain, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kliman et al., 2000 and Lachaise and Silvain, 2004

claim: D. simulans and D. sechellia diverged from each other approximately 0.5 MYA
source: These species diverged from D. melanogaster approximately 3–5 MYA and diverged from each other approximately 0.5 MYA (Kliman et al., 2000; Lachaise and Silvain, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kliman et al., 2000 and Lachaise and Silvain, 2004

claim: D. simulans larvae are less likely to form aggregations than are D. melanogaster larvae
source: These data are consistent with recent independent observations that D. simulans larvae are less likely to form aggregations than are D. melanogaster larvae (Durisko et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Durisko et al., 2014

claim: The reduced attractiveness of D. simulans is caused, at least in part, by a reduction in (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid production
source: First, the reduced attractiveness of D. simulans is caused, at least in part, by a reduction in (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid production.
evidence: Inferred from chemical analysis and behavioral data

claim: An unidentified repellent cue present in D. simulans residue blocks the attractive activity of the reduced levels of (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid
source: Second, an unidentified repellent cue present in D. simulans residue blocks the attractive activity of the reduced levels of (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid, and may act through a (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid-dependent mechanism to block larval attraction to (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral experiments with extracts and synthetic pheromones

claim: Interactions between pheromones that cause behaviorally antagonistic effects have been studied most intensively in the context of plume following during moth courtship
source: Interactions between pheromones that cause behaviorally antagonistic effects, such as we have observed, have been studied most intensively in the context of plume following during moth courtship (Baker, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baker, 2008

claim: In many moth species, female moths release blends of volatile attractive pheromones to attract courting males
source: In many species, female moths release blends of volatile attractive pheromones to attract courting males.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: The major components of moth pheromone blends are often shared in closely related sympatric species, while these blends differ in minor components
source: The major components of these blends are often shared in closely related sympatric species of moths, while these blends differ in minor components.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Species-specific minor components in moth pheromone blends can block the attraction of males to the blend
source: These species-specific minor components can block the attraction of males to the blend (Vickers and Baker, 1992; Quero and Baker, 1999; Lelito et al., 2008), a mechanism that likely reduces interspecific courtship.
evidence: Supported by citations to Vickers and Baker, 1992; Quero and Baker, 1999; Lelito et al., 2008

claim: The ratio of (Z)-5-tetradecenoic acid to (Z)-7-tetradecenoic acid is not significantly different between D. simulans, D. sechellia and D. melanogaster
source: We believe that this explanation is unlikely, because, although the levels of both pheromones are reduced in D. simulans, the ratio of these two pheromones is not significantly different from the ratios observed in D. sechellia and D. melanogaster (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6C

claim: Aggregation could lead to an increase in intra-specific competition over food sources
source: For example, aggregation could lead to an increase in intra-specific competition over food sources, which may outweigh the density-dependent advantage larvae experience while clustered.
evidence: Based on speculation about evolutionary costs and benefits

claim: The costs associated with providing positional information by releasing pheromones include increased risks of predation, parasitism, or cannibalism by conspecific larvae
source: Alternatively, the costs associated with providing positional information by releasing pheromones, such as the increased risks of predation, parasitism, or even cannibalism by conspecific larvae (Hassell, 2000; Vijendravarma et al., 2013) might in some situations outweigh the benefits of aggregation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hassell, 2000 and Vijendravarma et al., 2013

claim: The geographic range of D. simulans is largely overlapping with other species in this subgroup
source: Finally, the geographic range of D. simulans is largely overlapping with other species in this subgroup, and larvae of different species can often be found exploiting the same resource.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Drosophila ecology

claim: D. simulans larvae could benefit from eavesdropping on aggregation signals produced by other species while avoiding the direct and indirect costs of producing these compounds themselves
